checks.label: The current wave has a "head start" on the voltage wave; the current leads the voltage, and the voltage lags behind the current: on every AC screen each top and bottom of the drawn current comes a quarter cycle before the drawn voltage's

Capacitive reactance can be calculated using this formula: X_C = 1/(2πfC). The drawn X_C curve, its dot and the supply's peak ÷ the current's peak all agree with it at every setting of the frequency slider
Capacitive reactance decreases with increasing frequency: the drawn X_C curve falls all the way from 25 Hz to 100 Hz, and twice the frequency gives half the reactance and twice the current

Capacitors oppose changes in voltage by drawing or supplying current as they charge or discharge: while the drawn charge piles grow the current flows onto the charged plates, and while they shrink it flows back out

Power is never returned to the source by a resistive load, as it is with reactive loads: the capacitor's drawn power, the drawn voltage × the drawn current at each instant, goes below zero and averages zero, while the heater's never goes below zero
60 Hz is the most common frequency adopted for use on board ship: answered, the ship screen runs the capacitor at 60 Hz, where X_C is 8.33 Ω and the current peaks at 12 A

UK mains electricity operates at a nominal voltage of 230V: a 100 µF capacitor on 230 V, 50 Hz has X_C ≈ 31.8 Ω and draws 7.23 A; the capacitor drawing 2 A has X_C = 115 Ω, and on 60 Hz 95.8 Ω and 2.4 A

The capacitor's current is its capacitance × the steepness of its voltage: 10 A at 0 ms where the tangent is steepest, 0 A at 5 ms where it lies flat, −10 A at 10 ms; every drawn current point is C × the drawn voltage's slope there
At 0 ms the tangent gets steeper as the frequency rises, so the current peaks at 5 A on 25 Hz, 10 A on 50 Hz, 12 A on 60 Hz and 20 A on 100 Hz, and the flow arrows grow with it
The charge piles follow the voltage, as a capacitor holds C × its voltage, and the flow arrows follow the current: their length is its size, they turn round with it, and none crosses the gap
On 50 Hz the capacitor's power rises to 500 W and dips to −500 W, two humps up and two down each 20 ms cycle

On a steady 100 V the plates fill once and then draw no current: the drawn rush carries exactly C × 100 V of charge, the current ends at 0 A with the piles full, X_C climbs off the top of its graph and lesson 4's X_L reaches 0 Ω
